text: Where does the sugar you eat go?
Starch starts breaking down in your mouth, with an enzyme in your saliva.
Then it passes through your stomach.
In your small intestine, pancreatic amylase does the heavy lifting.
Brush border enzymes finish the job, leaving glucose, fructose and galactose.
These simple sugars pass into the blood in your villi.
That blood goes to your liver first, through the hepatic portal vein.
Your liver stores extra glucose as glycogen.
As blood sugar rises, beta cells in your pancreas release insulin.
Insulin helps your muscle and fat cells take glucose in.
Your kidneys filter glucose out of your blood all day long.
Then they pull almost all of it back.
That's why urine normally has almost no glucose.
